 19 
Note that ChatGPT did not change the ethos of the story to accommodate space aliens as it did in the 
second version of the XP-708-DQ story (p. 12). Perhaps it regarded space aliens as being compatible with 
an otherwise medieval ethos (knights and castle). Note also the phrase I’ve colored in aquamarine. It is 
in the Plan/Transit slot in one story and the Enact slot in another. Again, I take that as an indication that 
the distinction between trajectory segments is fuzzy and sometimes does not map well onto digital 
distinctions imposed on a language string by writing. 
Reverse Engineering ChatGPT 
I have the vague sense that somewhere I’ve read that the concept of reverse engineering was 
introduced into cognitive psychology by Donald Broadbent sometime perhaps as long ago as the 1950s, 
but certainly by the 1960s. Unfortunately I cannot provide a citation for that. Perhaps my mind is playing 
tricks on me, “hallucinating” as they say in the deep learning trade. But Steven Pinker makes a big deal 
of it in his book, How the Mind Works (1997, p. 21). Here’s what Pinker says: 
 
Reverse-engineering is what the boffins at Sony do when a new product is announced by 
Panasonic, or vice versa. They buy one, bring it back to the lab, take a screwdriver to it, and try 
to figure out what all the parts are for and how they combine to make the device work. We all 
engage in reverse-engineering when we face an interesting new gadget. 
 
That’s what the researchers at Anthropic had in mind when they discovered induction heads (p. 5). They 
are proponents of mechanistic interpretability. So am I. The purpose of this coda is to explain how this 
work contributes to that enterprise. 
 
The important thing to understand is that the behavior of complex systems, such as computer systems, 
and brains, need to be analyzed and described on several levels. David Marr and Thomas Poggio offered 
one such argument in the 1970s,11 which I have recently referenced.12 You can also consult Peter 
Gärdenfor’s work on conceptual spaces13 and a recent account by David Chapman.14 I propose that we 
think of ChatGPT ‘s behavior as being structured on three levels which we can call – the terms don’t 
matter – surface, middle, and bottom. 
 
I have been working with the surface level behavior – my prompts and ChatGPT’s responses – in this 
paper. The behavior looks more or less like the language behavior of human beings. That is not 
surprising. The value of neural network technology is that it can take on the appearances of a wide 
variety of behaviors. That in turn suggests that we can analyze and describe that behavior in terms that 
we use for human behavior. That is what I am doing when I describe these my example stories as being 
constructed on three levels.

 20 
At the bottom level we find an “exotic virtual machine,” to borrow a phrase from Chris Olah, 15 that is 
encoded in the transformer architecture. ChatGPT’s 175 billion parameters and their overall 
arrangement are specified at this level, but not their weights. Those weights are created during training 
and they encode ChatGPT’s middle level processes. When people refer to deep learning systems as 
“black boxes” or as being “opaque,” they are referring to these middle level processes. Induction heads 
belong to this middle level. They are not part of the transformer architecture. No one programmed 
them. Rather, they arise during the training process.16 
 
When I say that a certain class of stories is organized on three levels – story trajectory, segments in the 
trajectory, and sentences in the segments – I am describing a top-level phenomenon. That is a 
statement about stories, not about the processes that implement stories. The story process is 
implemented by processes encoded in patterns of parameter weights. Those processes, in turn, are 
implemented in the token generation process specified by the transformer architecture. 
 
The phenomenon of story coherence is an attribute of stories. I have identified three aspects of 
coherence: 1) protagonists act in ways in accordance with their essence (p. 3), 2) the ethos of the story 
must be consistent with the nature of the protagonist (p. 13), and 3) the protagonist must be the kind of 
thing one can tell a story about (p. 14) – which a colorless idea is not. There is nothing profound or 
particularly interesting about any of these; they seem obvious. But they are aspects of coherence, which 
no doubt has other aspects as well.  
 
Stories are realized through sentences and sentences through words. The order of those words, and 
Aspects of the Theory of Syntax Noam Chomsky famously distinguished between linguistic competence 
and linguistic performance. Here is what David Hays wrote about that distinction in a review article on 
computational linguistics that we coauthored: 
 
To describe an assembled bicycle is one thing: to describe the assembly of bicycles is another. 
The assembler must know what is in the blueprint (competence), but further needs the skill to 
take the parts in order, place them deftly, fasten them neatly (performance). In actuality, of 
course, the assembler may never have seen the blueprint, nor need the performance of a 
speaker or hearer include in any physical sense the grammar that the linguist offers as the 
blueprint of a language. 17 
 
That distinction allowed Chomsky to treat syntax as being formally well-formed, in the manner of a 
logical or mathematical expression, while making room for the fact that actual speech is often ill-
formed, full of interruptions and hesitations, and incomplete. Those imperfections belong to the realm 
of performance while syntax itself is in the realm of competence.  
 
It is linguistic performance that interests us, but not performance by humans. We are dealing with 
performance by a machine. While the sentences themselves belong in the surface level of ChatGPT’s 
behavior along with the three-level story structure, the mechanisms that produce them are in the

 21 
middle level, where they are encoded in patterns of weights on parameters. Recent work by Christopher 
D. Manning et al. 18 indicates that neural networks induce 
 
representations of sentence structure which capture many of the notions of linguistics, 
including word classes (parts of speech), syntactic structure (grammatical relations or 
dependencies), and coreference (which mentions of an entity refer to the same entity, such as, 
e.g., when “she” refers back to “Rachel”). [...] Indeed, the learned encoding of a sentence to a 
large extent includes the information found in the parse tree structures of sentences that have 
been proposed by linguists. 
 
Finally, considere the two conjectures I have offered: 1) these stories are generated through a nested 
hierarchy of probability distributions (p. 5), and 2) the degree of difference between a before-after pair 
of stories is proportional to the difference between the old and new protagonist or antagonist (p. 6). 
Those conjectures are about processes enacted through the pattern of weights in those 175 billion 
parameters. They belong to the middle level processes, along with induction heads. 
 
Those conjectures are just that, conjectures. I offer no direct evidence in favor of them. That these 
stories are organized on three levels is a matter of straight-forward description. The conjecture about 
nested distributions is derived from the application of that description to the fact that probability 
distributions change from token to token as the story is generated. Similarly, the conjecture about the 
relationship between differences between key characters (protagonist or antagonist) and differences 
between stories is based on intuitions about similarities between characters, on the one hand, and 
eyeballing the amount of yellow highlighting in the stories,19 on the other.  
 
That’s not rocket science, is it? But then I am not trying to land humans on the moon. I am speculating. 
My goal is to give my colleagues something worth thinking about, something that can be refined 
through observation and further thought.
